[Thinking]
**Generating a news-style story**

I need to create a story using the provided beginning sentences, ensuring it's in a news-like format and wrapped in double quotation marks. It’s crucial to avoid a verbatim continuation of copyrighted text; I can't continue beyond 90 characters. I want to produce an original story inspired by what the user provided but without directly reproducing large sections of text. So, I'll focus on crafting something new while respecting copyright guidelines!**Crafting a narrative**

I want to create a narrative that mixes human-interest elements with an institutional critique regarding police in NT, focusing on coroner findings and the history of failed CCTV installations in caged vans. This centers around the tragic death of 23-year-old Dale Scott Walkinshaw after a crash and detention. It's important to fictionalize details to avoid real-world defamatory claims. I’ll aim for a length of around 700-900 words and incorporate scenes featuring various characters, like the coroner and the deceased's mother, while using quotes for authenticity.
[/Thinking]

"By the time the coroner finished speaking, the courtroom air felt heavy, silted with a truth too long ignored. The words were simple and sharp — failed to act, ignored warnings, a death inevitable as a tide — and they folded over themselves in the minds of those listening until they felt like edges. A mother gripped a handkerchief crossed with forget-me-nots and stared at the bench as though it were the mouth of a tunnel she had no choice but to walk through.

Outside, dry heat lifted off the car park. In the distance, a plane banked over pale sky and the mangroves.

They had said it was a question of time. Not if, but when.

One of the constables who had been on duty the night of the crash — he was younger than most in the gallery expected — stood on the stone steps when it was done, jacket over his arm, shirt clinging damp beneath. He kept glancing at the lot where the police vehicles gleamed, white and without blame. He could see one of the vans, rear doors squared off like a shipping container, and for the first time since he joined the service he couldn’t meet his own reflection in the panel. He had sat awake too many nights since September, seeing rope, belts, shirts wound into cords; seeing hands slip and the quiet after. Six times they hadn’t been detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious, the report had said. He remembered each of those lines the way one remembers a bruise.

He and his partner had been en route to a noise complaint down Bagot Road — a Friday, half the city soft with end-of-week relief — when the crash lit the night ahead like summer lightning. He can still hear the puncture of it: glass, palm fronds rustling back into place. They pulled up to the Hilux nosed into the tree at the curve, and it was all dark around it, like the road had been swallowed. They found the young man — twenty-three, old enough to know better, he’d tell himself later; young enough to still forget that truth — half-hidden, a figure breathing hard through the smell of rum and eucalyptus. He cradled the passenger, pressing his cheek to her hair, whispering her name. When they coaxed him to stand, he looked up at them like he’d just remembered where he was.

He kept saying, She’s hurt. She can’t feel her legs. Please.

At the time there was only one thing to do: call the ambos, keep her still, keep him separate. He was unsteady, loud, grief and guilt making a hinge out of his voice. When the breath test came back glowing, just numbers and certainty, the procedure took over — transfer to the van, a note to check again later; their hands performing the duty long before thought could disrupt it. It wasn’t until they reached for the rear doors, brought to by habit to the metal cage, that the constable felt the old prickle again. He had read the internal report three years earlier as a fresh recruit: the recommendation for cameras in the vans, the list of incidents since the first death that should have forced a change. He had heard older officers joke about it — half cynicism, half gallows humor, most of it air — and he had caught his breath then, unsure where to put his own anger. If he was honest, he had learned not to ask.

The coroner said what the constable could not: This was foreseeable. This was preventable. When he said, It was a matter of when, the courtroom shifted in its seats, and a woman in the back who had once been held in the cage herself, for a night she still counted year by year, made a sound low enough that only those next to her turned to look.

The dead man’s name was spoken out loud again and again, the syllables settling into the carpet. Dale Scott Walkinshaw. His aunt had pinned a photo to her blouse — a boy with a crooked grin, the kind that suggests the future is a place you can just walk into if you step right. The crash was a page, not a book. He held the woman and did not run, she said afterwards. He stayed. She did not need to tell anyone that this was love, or cowardice undone, or simply what a person does when another is hurt. It hung there between them all, as heavy and complicated as any fact.

They brought in a detective from Professional Standards to account for the missed memo from 2013. It had gone to a working group; the funding line had been red-inked; a trial had been proposed and then delayed; the project officer took leave and did not come back; procurement was complicated. It sounded, in the saying, like weather. Like rain that did not fall because the clouds were misfiled.

But the files did not catch men in the act of tying their shirts to hooks along the steel seam of a van. The notes did not clatter onto the floor and bring back a person’s breath. The recommendations could not reach backward, into the dark, and place a lens where there had not been one.

There is something about a cage. Ask around town, and you will find there are people who still dream about the sound of the door closing, the way the light falls through the grate and stripes your thighs, how time loses weight and you can float out of yourself. Or down. They do not like to talk about it much. You learn to be quiet in the places where no one is watching. You learn that a scream is just a note, and notes do not make a song until someone listens.

In the weeks that followed the finding, the vans sprouted little black eyes in their backs — domes of plastic wired into the ceiling, lights winking red. It was easy, in the end. A contract signed, a screwdriver, an hour per vehicle. The memo could have been implemented between lunch and knock-off on a Tuesday three years earlier, one officer muttered to another, then felt the weight of his own meanness and stopped. Still, he wasn’t wrong.

The constable from that night began to run after his shifts, following the bike path that skirts the airport, the hum of the runway like a machine thinking. If he kept pace, he could stop the reels from turning in his head. If he reached the place where the path met the highway, he would turn and stand at the corner and stare at the palm tree. There are marks in bark that do not fade easily. He thought about saying sorry. He thought about the first time he’d been placed in charge of a van: the sweep of the torch across the cage, the dutiful test of the locks. He thought about all the faces that had sat there, humming with alcohol, grief, fear, bad timing; he thought about what any of them might have done given the tools and a dark and their own despair. He thought about how close a thing it is, to be alive.

On the morning the government announced a review into custodial protocols, a reporter found Dale’s mother at the shoreline where the mudflats burn pale. She did not speak in slogans. She did not curse the whole force. She said: My boy was not an angel. He was a person. He should have been seen. She buried her shoes in the cool mud and looked as though she might never move again.

There are stories that are just stories and there are stories that are warnings, and then there are the ones that are both and we do not listen until it is too late to keep the ending from happening. The coroner said as much without poetry: These events were predictable. He used a voice that asked no one’s permission to be heard. In the back row, a young officer who had not yet seen much closed his eyes against the sweat tickling his jaw and imagined pulling a lever in a room the size of a van. It makes a click, he thought. It turns something on. It shows you what has always been there.

After the inquest, the constable drove the long way home past the corner where the Hilux kissed the palm and left a scar. He rolled down the window and let all of Darwin in — the mango rot, the diesel, the salt. He slowed, just for a breath, and pulled over and got out. He placed his hand against the trunk. It was hot as a cheek. Thank you, he said, absurdly, to the tree. Then he looked up, past the crown’s green spray, to the endless, faithless blue, and felt the terrible, ordinary fact of being a person with hands and choices and a measure of power. He went back to his car. He turned the key. He drove on.

And the vans — those large white mouths — blinked their new eyes in the half-dark, and recorded, and did not forget."
